intro.why: This module sets the vocabulary and the data–model–loss–optimiser framing used in every later DNN module, from perceptrons (M2) through Transformers (M9) and optimisers (M10).
prereq: Basic ML ideas (supervised learning, features, labels)

sections.title: What is deep learning?
sections.plain: Multi-layer neural networks that extract progressively higher-level features.
sections.body:
• A type of machine learning based on artificial neural networks in which multiple layers of processing extract progressively higher-level features from data.
  • A method in AI that teaches computers to process data in a way inspired by the human brain.
  • A technique that teaches computers to do what comes naturally to humans: learn by example.
  • A subset of ML, essentially a neural network with three or more layers.
  • Named for adding more layers to learn from the data (p.4).

sections.title: Where in AI does DL sit?
sections.plain: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ NN ⊃ DL; data science overlaps.
sections.body: AI is the general field that encompasses ML and DL but also many approaches that involve no learning (search, logic, planning, rule-based expert systems). The slide's nested diagram (p.5): Artificial Intelligence ⊃ Machine Learning ⊃ Neural Networks ⊃ Deep Learning, with Data Science overlapping ML, NN and DL.

sections.title: AI, ML and DL defined
sections.body:
Definition (p.6)
AIThe science of making things smart: machines that perform human tasks, e.g. a robot cleaning a room.
MLAn approach to AI: the machine learns or performs tasks through learning by experience.
DLA technique for implementing machine learning to recognise patterns.

Mitchell's definition of learning fits all of ML: a program learns from experience E with respect to tasks T and performance measure P if its performance at T, measured by P, improves with E.

sections.title: Deep (machine) learning: successive representations
sections.plain: Depth = number of layers that contribute to the model.
sections.body:
Deep learning is a specific subfield of ML that learns representations from data with an emphasis on successive layers of increasingly meaningful representations. The "deep" stands for this idea of successive layers; the number of layers contributing to the model is its depth. The layered representations are learned via neural networks, structured in literal layers stacked on top of each other (p.7).

Formally a deep model is a composition $f(\mathbf x)=f^{(L)}(\cdots f^{(2)}(f^{(1)}(\mathbf x)))$ with $f^{(l)}(\mathbf h)=\sigma(W^{(l)}\mathbf h+\mathbf b^{(l)})$. Without the non-linearities σ the composition collapses to a single linear map, which is why depth needs non-linear activations (Module 5). Our NumPy run (code ex2) on two rings: no hidden layer 52% test accuracy, one hidden layer of 4 units 99.5%.

sections.title: Why deep learning?
sections.plain: Data, sensors, compute, storage, automatic features, scalability.
sections.body:
• Large amounts of data; lots of unstructured data (images, text, audio, video).
  • Cheap, high-quality sensors; cheap computation (CPU, GPU, distributed clusters); cheap data storage.
  • Learn by examples; automated feature generation (representation learning replaces manual feature engineering).
  • Better learning capabilities; scalability; advanced analytics can be applied (p.9).

sections.title: Scale drives deep learning progress
sections.plain: Bigger networks keep improving with more labelled data.
sections.body: Andrew Ng's figure (p.10): performance vs amount of labelled data for traditional ML (logistic regression, SVM, …), small, medium and large NNs. With small training sets the ranking is unclear (feature engineering dominates); as data grows, traditional algorithms plateau while larger networks continue to improve. Empirical "scaling laws" for modern models (e.g. Kaplan et al., 2020) quantify this: test loss falls approximately as a power law in data, parameters and compute, $L\approx(D_c/D)^{\alpha}$.

sections.title: Many more applications
sections.body:
• Predict tomorrow's weather from geographic information, satellite images and a trailing window of past weather.
  • Answer a free-form text question correctly.
  • Given an image, identify all the people it contains, drawing outlines around each (instance segmentation).
  • Present users with products they are likely to enjoy but unlikely to encounter by browsing (p.13).

sections.title: Core components of a DL problem
sections.body:
1. The data we can learn from.
  2. A model of how to transform the data.
  3. An objective function that quantifies how well (or badly) the model is doing.
  4. An algorithm to adjust the model's parameters to optimise the objective (p.15).

Diagram: Data → Learning Algorithm (containing the Loss Function) → Model. Written as an optimisation problem: $\theta^*=\arg\min_\theta\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\ell\big(f(\mathbf x^{(i)};\theta),t^{(i)}\big)$.

sections.title: 1. Data
sections.plain: D = {X, t}; N examples, d features.
sections.body:
Data are a collection of examples converted to a useful numerical representation. Each example (data point, instance, sample) consists of features (covariates); in supervised problems the attribute to predict is the label (target) (p.16). $\mathcal D=\{X,t\}$; number of features = number of dimensions = $d$; number of examples = $N$; more features means higher dimensionality (p.17). Example: houses with features Bedrooms, Location, Sq Ft and target Price:

IDBedroomsLocationSq FtPrice
13Urban1500350K
22Suburban1200280K
34Urban2000520K
43Rural1800310K
52Suburban1100245K
65Urban2500680K
73Rural1600275K
84Suburban1900425K

Here $N=8$, $d=3$. Location is categorical and must be encoded (one-hot) before a network can use it.

sections.title: 2. Model
sections.body: The model is the computational machinery for ingesting data of one type and producing predictions of a possibly different type. Deep learning models consist of many successive transformations of the data chained top to bottom, hence "deep" (p.18).

sections.title: 3. Objective function
sections.plain: Formal measure of how bad the model is; lower is better.
sections.body: Learning means improving at some task over time. Objective functions are formal measures of how good (or bad) a model is; by convention lower is better, so they are called loss functions (p.19). Common choices: squared error $\frac12(y-t)^2$ for regression, cross-entropy $-\sum_kt_k\log y_k$ for classification. The loss must usually be differentiable so that gradients can be computed.

sections.title: 4. Learning algorithms
sections.plain: Search for parameters minimising the loss: gradient descent.
sections.body: A learning algorithm searches for the best parameters minimising the loss; the popular algorithm for deep learning is gradient descent (p.20): $$\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta L(\theta).$$ In practice with mini-batches (SGD) and adaptive variants (Adam, Module 10). On the house table (code ex1), gradient descent on standardised features reaches the closed-form least-squares solution (loss 1295.6) after a few thousand steps.

sections.title: Example of the framework
sections.plain: Define inputs/outputs, choose a family, collect labelled data.
sections.body: We must tell a computer explicitly how to map inputs to outputs: define the problem precisely (exact nature of inputs and outputs), choose an appropriate model family, and collect a huge dataset of audio examples labelled as containing or not containing the wake word (p.21).

sections.title: How to create a model
sections.plain: A parameterised program tuned on data.
sections.body: Start with a program whose behaviour is determined by a number of parameters. Determine the best parameters using data (examples): parameters that improve the program's performance with respect to the loss (p.22).

sections.title: Train the model; families of models
sections.plain: Trained program = model; all reachable programs = family.
sections.body: Train the program with data to find the parameters that improve performance with respect to the loss; once the parameters are finalised we call the program a model (e.g. it receives an audio snippet and outputs yes/no). The set of all distinct programs (input–output mappings) obtainable by manipulating the parameters is a family of models: the same family should suit "Alexa" and "Hey Siri" recognition because the tasks are similar (p.23). This is the hypothesis space $\mathcal H=\{f(\cdot;\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}$.

sections.title: Learning problems
sections.body:
1. Supervised: training by examples; the dataset has data and labels; e.g. classification, regression.
  2. Unsupervised: a large dataset of features only; e.g. clustering, generating synthetic data (GANs), density estimation.
  3. Reinforcement: an agent interacts with an environment and takes actions over a series of time steps, learning from rewards (p.25).

Self-supervised learning (predicting masked or next tokens, Module 9) creates labels from the data itself and powers today's large models.

sections.title: Supervised learning
sections.plain: Map inputs to labels; learn P(label | features).
sections.body: The task of predicting labels given input features; each feature–label pair is an example; the goal is a model mapping any input to a label prediction. The supervision: we provide labelled examples, and the model estimates the conditional probability of a label given the input features, $P(t\mid\mathbf x)$ (p.26).

sections.title: Supervised learning tasks
sections.body:
• Regression: how much / how many.
  • Classification: binary, multi-class, multi-label.
  • Recommender systems.
  • Sequence learning: tagging and parsing, automatic speech recognition, text to speech, machine translation (p.27).

Typical output layers and losses: regression → linear output + squared error; binary → sigmoid + binary cross-entropy; multi-class → softmax + cross-entropy; multi-label → one sigmoid per label + binary cross-entropy each.

sections.title: Comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
Traditional MLDeep learning
FeaturesHand-engineeredLearned (representation learning)
Data neededWorks with small dataShines with large data
ComputeCPU, minutesGPU/TPU, hours to weeks
InterpretabilityOften higherLower (post-hoc XAI)
Best onTabular dataImages, audio, text, video
  • "Neural networks work like the brain." They are loosely inspired by neurons; real neurons and learning rules are far more complex.
  • "More layers is always better." Very deep plain networks are hard to train (vanishing gradients) and overfit without enough data; residual connections, normalisation and regularisation are needed.
  • "Gradient descent finds the global minimum." Neural-network losses are non-convex; GD finds good local minima/saddle regions.

code.title: The four components on the house table
code.explain: Data (N = 8, d = 2), a linear model, a squared-error loss and gradient descent, converging to the closed-form least-squares solution.
mistakes: Running gradient descent on raw square feet (scale ~1000s) without standardising: tiny learning rates and slow convergence.
code.notes: Standardisation makes the loss surface rounder, so one learning rate works for all parameters.
code.code:
# The four core components of a DL problem on the session's house table: data, model, loss, algorithm
import numpy as np
# 1. Data D = {X, t}: N examples, d features (bedrooms, sq ft); target = price in $K
X = np.array([[3, 1500], [2, 1200], [4, 2000], [3, 1800], [2, 1100], [5, 2500], [3, 1600], [4, 1900]], float)
t = np.array([350, 280, 520, 310, 245, 680, 275, 425], float)
N, d = X.shape; print(f"N = {N} examples, d = {d} features")
mu, sd = X.mean(0), X.std(0); Z = (X - mu) / sd          # numerical representation: standardised
# 2. Model: y = Z w + b (a family of models indexed by the parameters w, b)
w, b = np.zeros(d), 0.0
# 3. Objective (loss): mean squared error, lower is better
loss = lambda w, b: ((Z @ w + b - t) ** 2).mean() / 2
# 4. Learning algorithm: gradient descent
lr = 0.1
for step in range(3001):
    err = Z @ w + b - t
    if step in (0, 1, 5, 20, 200, 3000): print(f"step {step:3d}  loss = {loss(w, b):9.2f}  w = {np.round(w, 2)}  b = {b:.2f}")
    w -= lr * Z.T @ err / N; b -= lr * err.mean()
x_new = (np.array([3, 1700]) - mu) / sd; print("prediction for a 3-bedroom, 1700 sq ft house: $%.0fK" % (x_new @ w + b))
w_ls = np.linalg.lstsq(np.c_[Z, np.ones(N)], t, rcond=None)[0]; print("closed-form least squares:", np.round(w_ls, 2))
